question: In the light of the ongoing legal proceedings against the Saxony-Anhalt branch of the AfD and the associated measures taken by the secret services1 against the number one opposition party in the opinion polls, during a state election campaign no less, I have the following questions: 1.

What view does the European Commission take of the use of secret service resources to monitor an opposition party that is currently leading in the opinion polls? This is fundamentally a matter of whether such measures are compatible with democratic principles and the rights of the opposition, in particular with regard to Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union, which stresses the EU’s values and democracy.

The AfD has not yet been given access to the 134-page report, which makes a wellfounded judicial review considerably more difficult. How does the Commission view this course of action in view of the rights to an effective remedy and a fair trial enshrined in Article 47 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights?

How can the Commission ensure that such classifications and the associated intelligence surveillance comply with the rule of law and do not violate fundamental democratic rights? This includes, in particular, the protection of freedom of expression and political participation, as enshrined in Article 11 and Article 12 of the EU Charter of Fundamental Rights.
Supporters2
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (21.10.2024) Safeguarding democratic values is a key priority for the Commission. In this regard, the Commission has taken many measures to promote free and fair elections, including putting forward a Recommendation on inclusive and resilient elections1.

The Recommendation recognises that the use of surveillance can under certain conditions be a matter of national security and states that national security should be interpreted in compliance with the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union to preserve the effective application of the EU law.

The Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union applies to Member States only when they are implementing EU law, in line with its Article 51(1). Based on the information available, the situation described by the Honourable Member does not appear to fall within the scope of application of EU law.

In such cases, it is for Member States, including their judicial authorities, to ensure that fundamental rights are effectively respected and protected, in accordance with their national legislation and international human rights obligations. The European Commission promotes and protects the rule of law and carefully monitors the situation in all Member States, including Germany.
This is reflected in the recently adopted 2024 Rule of Law Report, including the country chapter on Germany2.
